**Before this page:** [interval arithmetic](interval-arithmetic.qmd),
[zonotopes](zonotopes.qmd) and [how the two work
together](intervals-and-zonotopes.qmd). The funnels themselves, edge by
edge, are on [certified funnels](funnels.qmd).

## 1. What a funnel is

**Intuition.** A feedback law steers the block along one piece of the plan
(one *edge*: a single contact formation with fixed stick or slip modes). A
**funnel** is a certified tube around the planned motion: every state that
starts in its **entry set** stays in the tube and leaves through its **exit
set**, for every disk friction in $[0.3,0.5]$ and every disturbance in a
measured set [@burridge1999sequential; @tedrake2010lqrtrees; @majumdar2017funnel].

**Check it by hand (a toy).** A rate error $\eta$ obeys
$\eta_{k+1}=0.5\,\eta_k+w_k$ with $|w_k|\le0.1$. Entry set
$|\eta_0|\le0.2$. Then $|\eta_1|\le0.5\cdot0.2+0.1=0.2$: the interval
$[-0.2,0.2]$ maps into itself, so it is a tube for every step, and any
condition that holds on it holds along the whole motion.

**The general statement.** The certificate checks, by
[interval](interval-arithmetic.qmd) or [zonotope](zonotopes.qmd)
arithmetic on the rigid model, that one step of the planned mode carries
every state of each band of the tube into a later band or the exit set,
and that at every such state:

- every closed contact carries a normal force of at least the **derived
  force floor** $N_{\min}=2\times10^{-4}$ N, the simulator's measured
  one-step contact-force residual at its joint 95/95 bound;
- every force lies in its **friction cone** (sliding contacts on the edge
  opposite the slip, sticking ones strictly inside an inner cone);
- the **motor forces** lie in their box;
- the **recognizer reads** the planned formation with margin.

The executed motion is then checked in MJX on held-out rollouts.

## 2. Utilization: how much room is left

**Intuition.** Each condition has a margin: how far the worst state in the
set is from violating it. **Utilization** is the certificate's smallest
remaining margin as a fraction of its capacity. **1 means untouched, 0
means at the limit: higher is safer.**

**Check it by hand.** A friction cone allows $|f_t|\le\mu f_n$. If over the
whole tube $|f_t|\le0.6\,\mu f_n$, that condition's utilization is
$1-0.6=0.4$. If another condition's is $0.25$, the certificate's
utilization is $0.25$, set by the tighter one, its **binding** condition.

**In our chain.** The roll from $62^\circ$ is certified at 0.376, bound by
the step corner's cone edge; the platform transport at about 0.21, bound by
a force floor.

## 3. Choosing a law: coverage first, then utilization

**Intuition.** First make sure the law handles *every* state it must
(coverage); among those that do, take the one with the most room
(largest utilization). Coverage is judged for the **chain**, not the edge
alone.

**Check it by hand.** Three push magnitudes after the roll, each certified
on $2\times8$ sub-boxes of the roll's certified exit set (a single tube over
the whole exit set is refused at every magnitude):

| push | sub-boxes certified | utilization |
|---|---|---|
| 0.0538 N | 16 of 16 | 0.488 |
| 0.1116 N | 16 of 16 | 0.686 |
| 0.2316 N | 16 of 16 | 0.316 |

All three cover the roll's exit; 0.1116 N has the largest utilization and
is chosen, provided its landing also passes (next paragraph).

**Why coverage is the chain's.** A push counts only if the *landing after
it* also comes to rest in the planned formation, because a stronger push
lands harder. The landings after the 0.1116 N push hit the platform at
34.5–35.5°/s; with the ray-0 roll's 0.02531 N push they hit at
13.7–17.9°/s. Both came to rest in every MJX rollout (1536 of 1536), so
both pass the chain's coverage test.

## 4. Composition: on certified sets only

**Intuition.** Two funnels chain when everything the first can deliver is
something the second has been proved to accept. Both sides must be
*proved* sets.

**Check it by hand.** Funnel A's certified exit is $\eta\in[-0.05,0.04]$.
Funnel B's certified entry is $\eta\in[-0.06,0.06]$. Since
$[-0.05,0.04]\subseteq[-0.06,0.06]$, the junction composes. If B's entry
were only *measured*, say the 95/95 region of the speeds MJX happened to
produce, it would not count: a measured set describes what was executed,
not what is guaranteed.

**The general statement.** A junction composes [@burridge1999sequential] when the exit set certified
for one edge lies in the entry set certified for the next (the next
funnel's bands re-verified from it). **Measured entry sets are subsets of
the executed states and are used only to validate coverage; composition is
established on certified sets.** The end-to-end claim is the per-certificate
claims combined by a union bound: with $m$ certificates each holding except
with probability $\alpha_i$, the chain holds except with probability at
most $\sum_i\alpha_i$, with the measured end-to-end coverage reported
alongside.

### The automatic check, and a cascade

A script, `chain_check`, reads each junction's exported set records and
passes it only if the certified exit lies inside the certified entry,
compared exactly. A measured set fails as **FAIL (measured)**, a missing
record as **FAIL (missing)**, and a NaN never passes.

**A cascade.** Re-certifying the tip from its departure's certified hand-off
widened the tip's exit by about $10^{-5}$ rad/s: $|\eta'|\le0.036055$
against the pivot's certified entry $0.036045$ rad/s, and $0.200$ mm against
$0.182$ mm in the disk's place. That is outside, so the pivot was
re-verified from the new exit (it holds, utilization 0.228), and the stop
after it was re-certified from the pivot's new exit. A one-line change at
the start of the chain forces every downstream junction to be re-checked,
which is exactly what an automatic check is for.

### "Inside the band" is not "a certified entry"

Landing inside a funnel's certified *bands* does not by itself make a
certified entry: the bands are proved invariant only for states that enter
through the funnel's entry set. A departure that ends in the bands but
outside the entry set needs the funnel **re-verified from that departure's
exit**. Until then, `chain_check` fails the junction.

### Asymmetric entry sets

**Intuition.** A box entry set is symmetric about its centre. If the motion
only goes forward, a symmetric box admits states that go *backwards*, which
no real departure produces, and the certificate refuses them.

**In our chain.** The floor-corner lift's departure hands off at a tilt
rate within $[-0.0039,+0.0286]$ rad/s of its target of 1°/s (0.0175 rad/s).
A symmetric entry of $\pm0.0286$ rad/s includes rates below
$-0.0175$ rad/s about the target, i.e. tilting backwards, and the funnel
refused it (no progress). Re-verified from the asymmetric entry, it holds
(utilization 0.267).

## 5. Measured quantities: joint 95/95 bounds

**Intuition.** A certificate needs bounds on what the simulator does that
the rigid model does not (residual accelerations, creep, settling). Bounding
each quantity separately at 95/95 does *not* give 95% coverage of the whole
certificate, because a rollout must lie inside all bounds at once.

**Check it by hand.** Five independent quantities, each inside its own
bound 95% of the time: all five at once only about $0.95^5=77\%$ of the
time.

**The general statement.** One **joint** region, built from order statistics
[@wilks1941determination; @krishnamoorthy2009statistical]: each quantity is centred at
its median and scaled by its own order statistic on half the calibration
rollouts; one common inflation is the order statistic of the largest scaled
deviation on the other half. It covers at least 95% of rollouts in all
quantities at once, with 97.5% confidence per end of the friction band (so
both ends hold at 95%). On the tip, per-quantity bounds covered 882 of 1000
held-out rollouts jointly; the joint region covered 963.

**Bound each quantity where it lives.** Charging the largest creep measured
anywhere to every contact point over-bounds the contacts that barely move.
On the roll from $62^\circ$, the disk's place on the bottom face creeps up to
2.39 mm in MJX, the largest creep of any contact. Charging 2.39 mm to the
step-corner contact as well made the first band's lower bound on progress per step $-2.9\times10^{-5}$,
a refusal; with each contact's own creep it is at least
$1.37\times10^{-4}$, above the $3.49\times10^{-5}$ one band needs, and the
roll certifies. Each contact carries its own bound inside the joint
region.

**The rigid-versus-simulator gap is a measured disturbance.** After the
make under the bottom face, MJX's block settles $+0.473$ to $+0.489^\circ$ in
tilt (and $+0.885$ to $+0.907$ mm in the step corner's place) relative to the
rigid model's rest. That settle enters the next departure's start set as a
measured joint 95/95 region.

## 6. Execute end to end, not just segment by segment

**Intuition.** Checking each segment in its own simulation, from states
saved by the previous one, can miss what happens between segments and
whether the whole chain reaches the task's goal.

**In our chain.** One continuous MJX simulation per rollout, 1536 rollouts
from the block at rest to the platform transport's exit: every segment
survived in all 1536, and the chain's own goal was reached in all 1536
(Clopper–Pearson [@clopper1934use] 95%: $[0.9976,1]$). But the executor also evaluates goal
tests that no segment check looks at, and the stricter one, `lift_to`, was
met in none of the 1536 runs: the platform transport's certified exit lies
at 42.07 mm along the platform, short of where that test passes. A
transport certified on to 62.4 mm, the first section passing the lift goal
test (utilization 0.2083, 757 of 757 held-out rollouts inside), is the edge
that addresses it.

## What to remember

- A **funnel**: entry set, law and tube, a certificate (force floor, cones,
  motor box, reading condition) on the rigid model, checked in MJX.
- **Utilization**: the smallest remaining margin as a fraction of capacity;
  1 untouched, 0 at the limit, **higher is safer**.
- **Choose** by coverage of the whole chain first, then the largest
  utilization.
- **Compose on certified sets only**; measured sets validate coverage;
  the end-to-end claim is a union bound over certificates.
- `chain_check` makes the containment automatic; a change upstream
  cascades downstream.
- **Inside the band is not a certified entry**; prefer **asymmetric**
  entry sets for one-directional motion.
- Measured quantities as **joint 95/95** regions, per contact, including
  the rigid-versus-simulator settle.
- **Execute end to end**: it finds gaps that segment checks miss.

Next: [the techniques that made the chain certify](certification-techniques.qmd).

## Further reading {.unnumbered}

- Burridge, Rizzi and Koditschek [@burridge1999sequential]: the classic on sequential composition of funnels, where "exit inside the next entry" comes from.
- Tedrake et al. [@tedrake2010lqrtrees]: LQR-trees, funnels verified by sums of squares and composed into a tree.
- Majumdar and Tedrake [@majumdar2017funnel]: funnel libraries composed online, with robustness to disturbances.
- Sadraddini and Tedrake [@sadraddini2019linear]: linear encodings for the containment checks a junction needs.
- Wilks [@wilks1941determination]: distribution-free tolerance limits from order statistics, the basis of a 95/95 bound.
- Krishnamoorthy and Mathew [@krishnamoorthy2009statistical]: tolerance regions in depth, including multivariate and nonparametric ones.
- Clopper and Pearson [@clopper1934use] and Wilson [@wilson1927probable]: exact and score confidence intervals for a success rate such as 1536 of 1536.
- McNemar [@mcnemar1947note]: the paired test used to compare two configurations on the same starts.
